items.prompt:
Analyze this description: 'The old man walks with a cane, wears a red sweater every Monday, and whistles the same song every morning as he waters his rose bushes.'

List FOUR specific details and explain what type of detail each one is (appearance, behavior, habit, sensory).
items.answer: 1. 'Walks with a cane' — appearance/physical behavior. 2. 'Wears a red sweater every Monday' — clothing/habit. 3. 'Whistles the same song every morning' — sensory (sound) + habit. 4. 'Waters his rose bushes' — behavioral detail (what he does).

steps: Detail 1: cane — physical appearance, tells us about mobility.
Detail 2: red sweater on Mondays — specific clothing + repetitive habit.
Detail 3: whistles same song — sound detail + habit (routine).
Detail 4: waters rose bushes — action detail (shows what he does each morning).

items.prompt: A student describes her best friend using ONLY vague words: 'She is nice, fun, and smart.' Rewrite this description using SHOW-NOT-TELL — replace each vague word with a specific, concrete detail that demonstrates the quality.
items.answer: Example: 'She shares her snack without being asked (nice). She invents games for us to play at recess every day (fun). She figured out how to solve the hardest puzzle in our classroom before anyone else (smart).'

steps: 'Nice' → show it: 'shares her snack without being asked.'
'Fun' → show it: 'invents games for us to play at recess every day.'
'Smart' → show it: 'solved the hardest puzzle in class before anyone else.'
Show-not-tell: replace adjectives with specific actions or behaviors that demonstrate the quality.

items.prompt:
Compare these two descriptions of a hurricane:
A) 'It was a very bad storm.'
B) 'The wind screamed at 120 miles per hour, bending palm trees sideways until their fronds scraped the ground. Rain came in horizontal sheets, and the sky turned a sickly green color.'

Identify ALL the types of sensory and specific details used in Option B.
items.answer: Sound: wind screamed. Quantitative detail: 120 miles per hour. Visual: trees bending sideways, fronds scraping ground, sky turned sickly green. Tactile/directional: rain came in horizontal sheets. Each detail is specific and creates a vivid, dramatic picture.

steps: Sound: 'wind screamed' (personification + sound).
Specific number: '120 miles per hour' — gives measurable precision.
Visual: 'bending palm trees sideways' + 'fronds scraped the ground.'
Color/visual: 'sky turned a sickly green.'
Tactile/movement: 'rain came in horizontal sheets.'

items.prompt: Write a 3-sentence description of a moment when you felt very surprised. Use: (1) a sensory detail, (2) a specific action showing your surprise, and (3) a specific detail about what caused the surprise. (Write as if giving this as a spoken presentation.)
items.answer: Example: 'When I walked into the living room, the lights were off and everything was silent — then the lights came on and thirty people yelled SURPRISE! My heart leaped into my throat and I jumped back against the wall. They had hidden behind the couch for an hour, holding balloons that said my name in big gold letters.'

steps: Sensory detail: silence + lights off, then sudden light and loud voices.
Specific action showing surprise: 'heart leaped into my throat and I jumped back against the wall.'
Specific cause: 'hidden behind the couch for an hour, holding balloons with my name in gold.'

items.prompt:
A student is asked to describe a historical event — the first moon landing — for her class. She should include: what happened, sensory details (as if you were there), how people felt, and one specific fact.

Write a strong 3-4 sentence description.
items.answer: Example: 'On July 20, 1969, astronaut Neil Armstrong stepped off a ladder onto the surface of the moon — the first human ever to touch it. The surface was gray and powdery, and Armstrong's boot left a perfect print in the dust. Back on Earth, millions of people crowded around black-and-white television sets, holding their breath, then erupting in tears and cheers. Armstrong said, "That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind."'

steps: Event: Neil Armstrong lands on the moon (July 20, 1969).
Sensory: gray, powdery surface; boot print; millions watching TV.
Feeling: holding breath, tears and cheers.
Specific fact: quote from Armstrong.

items.prompt: Explain the difference between 'telling' feelings and 'showing' feelings in a description. Give one example of each for the feeling of excitement.
items.answer: Telling: 'I was excited.' — just labels the emotion. Showing: 'I could not sit still — I kept jumping out of my seat, and my hands were shaking so much I could barely tie my shoes.' — shows the physical and behavioral signs of excitement without using the word.

steps: Telling: states the emotion directly with a label.
Showing: describes physical reactions and behaviors that signal the emotion.
Showing is more vivid and engaging for the listener.

items.prompt: A student describes her community garden for show-and-tell. She includes: its location, what grows there, two sensory details, and how the community uses it. Write a strong description combining all four elements.
items.answer: Example: 'Our community garden is on the corner of Maple Street, right behind the library. Tall sunflowers line the front, and the tomato plants are so heavy with fruit they need sticks to hold them up. On Saturdays, families come together to weed and water — the whole garden smells like earth and fresh basil. Last week, we harvested enough zucchini to share with every family on the block.'

steps: Location: corner of Maple Street, behind the library.
What grows: sunflowers, tomatoes, zucchini, basil.
Sensory: smell of earth and fresh basil; heavy tomato plants needing stakes.
Community use: families come Saturdays to weed/water; harvest shared with families.

items.prompt: What is the difference between a GENERAL detail and a SPECIFIC detail? Give an example of each for describing a teacher.
items.answer: General: 'My teacher is kind.' (vague — any teacher could be described this way.) Specific: 'My teacher writes encouraging notes on my homework and always remembers my dog's name when I mention her.' (unique and concrete — only this specific teacher does these things.)

steps: General details could describe almost anyone or anything.
Specific details are unique, concrete, and observable — they point to the exact person, place, or thing.
In descriptions, specific details are far more effective because they help the listener form a precise mental picture.

items.prompt: A student is asked to describe her city for someone who has never visited. She must include: geography, something unique, a sensory detail, and a feeling. Write the description.
items.answer: Example: 'My city sits right where the river bends, so from the bridge you can see the water go in two directions. What makes it unique is the giant bronze statue of a leaping fish in the town square — every kid in town has climbed on it at least once. The air near the waterfront always smells like wet rocks and rain. When I walk downtown after school, I feel like the whole city is mine to explore.'

steps: Geography: where the river bends; bridge view.
Unique: giant bronze fish statue in town square.
Sensory: smell of wet rocks and rain near waterfront.
Feeling: sense of ownership and adventure walking downtown.

items.prompt:
Why is it important to include relevant feelings when describing an event — not just what happened?
A) Feelings are not important; only facts matter.
B) Feelings help the listener connect personally to the event, making the description more vivid, memorable, and honest.
items.answer: B) Feelings help the listener connect personally to the event, making the description more vivid, memorable, and honest.

steps: Facts alone are informative but can be dry.
Feelings add a human dimension that helps the listener relate.
Honest feelings also show what the event meant to the speaker — why it was worth describing.
CCSS 1.SL.B.4 specifically calls for 'expressing ideas and feelings clearly.'

items.prompt: A student's description of a museum visit has 6 sentences. Three use only general words ('big,' 'cool,' 'a lot'). The other three use specific details. She is told to revise the three vague sentences. What should she do?
items.answer: She should replace each vague word with specific, observable details. For 'big': describe the actual size or give a comparison ('tall as a four-story building'). For 'cool': describe what exactly was interesting ('a meteor the size of a refrigerator'). For 'a lot': give a specific number or type ('hundreds of fossils sorted by era').

steps: 'Big' → use a comparison or measurement.
'Cool' → describe the specific thing that made it interesting.
'A lot' → give a number or specific type.
Revision goal: every sentence should paint a specific picture.

items.prompt: Design a checklist with FOUR criteria a student should check before presenting a description. Explain what each criterion means.
items.answer: 1. Specific details: Have I replaced vague words with concrete observations? 2. Sensory language: Did I include what I see, hear, smell, taste, or feel? 3. Relevance: Does every detail directly relate to the topic? 4. Feelings: Did I show (not just tell) how I felt or how others reacted?

steps: Criterion 1: Specificity — no vague words like 'nice,' 'good,' or 'fun.'
Criterion 2: Sensory — five senses engaged where appropriate.
Criterion 3: Relevance — cut anything that does not directly describe the topic.
Criterion 4: Feelings — show feelings through actions and reactions, not just labels.

items.prompt: A student says: 'The ocean was pretty.' Expand this into a 3-sentence description using all five senses.
items.answer: Example: 'The ocean glittered like broken glass in the afternoon sun, and the waves crashing on shore sounded like a continuous rumble of thunder. The air tasted salty on my lips, and the cold spray hit my face every time a big wave broke. I dug my feet into the wet sand, which felt icy and gritty between my toes.'

steps: Sight: glittered like broken glass.
Sound: waves sounded like thunder.
Taste: air tasted salty.
Touch (face): cold spray.
Touch (feet): icy, gritty sand.

items.prompt:
Compare two descriptions of meeting a new friend:
A) 'She was nice and we got along well.'
B) 'She walked up and said, "I like your drawing" — and that was it. We spent the whole recess drawing in my sketchbook, taking turns making up characters for a story. By the time the bell rang, I already knew her favorite color, her dog's name, and that she could whistle with her fingers.'
items.answer: B is far stronger. It shows the friendship forming through specific moments and dialogue rather than labeling it as 'nice.' The reader can picture exactly how the friendship started and what made it special.

steps: Option A: tells that they got along well but shows nothing specific.
Option B: shows how they got along (drawing together, talking, sharing) through specific actions and dialogue.
The reader can almost feel what this friendship is like from Option B's details alone.

items.prompt: What does CCSS standard 1.SL.B.4 require students to do when describing people, places, things, and events? List ALL four required elements from the standard.
items.answer: The standard requires: (1) describing people, places, things, and events; (2) using relevant details; (3) expressing ideas clearly; (4) expressing feelings clearly.

steps: Element 1: Describe — give an account of a person, place, thing, or event.
Element 2: Relevant details — details must directly relate to the subject.
Element 3: Express ideas clearly — the description should make sense and be organized.
Element 4: Express feelings clearly — the speaker's feelings about the subject should be included.
